Errand Agent: AI shopping agent with PayPal guardrails

An AI shopping agent with spending guardrails and PayPal Sandbox checkout. The AI proposes, the policy engine decides, the human approves, and the server charges. Built for the PayPal AI Hackathon.

 Like  Comment
STORY
UPDATES
SUBMISSION HISTORY

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
Inspiration

Everyone wants an AI that can handle everyday errands, but very few people would feel comfortable giving an AI unrestricted access to their payment methods.

I wanted to solve this trust problem. Instead of building another shopping chatbot, I set out to create an AI shopping agent that can genuinely help users find products and prepare purchases while being structurally unable to spend money on its own.

My central idea was simple: The LLM proposes, the policy engine decides, the human approves, and the server charges.

What it does

Errand Agent lets users describe shopping requests in natural language, such as:

"Find my sister a birthday gift under $60."

The agent searches the product catalog, builds a shopping cart, and submits it to a deterministic policy engine. The engine checks the cart against configurable rules:

Per-order spending limit
Monthly budget limit
Restricted product categories
Maximum item limit
Currency restrictions

If the cart passes every check, the user sees an approval card and can pay through PayPal Sandbox checkout.

If the cart violates a rule, the purchase is blocked. The system explains which rule was hit, shows the relevant numbers, and lets the agent propose a compliant alternative.

Every important action and policy decision is recorded in a live ledger that users can sort, filter and inspect.

How I built it

I built Errand Agent with Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SQLite, AG Grid Community, Zod and Vitest.

The AI agent uses Groq's OpenAI-compatible API (open-weight model openai/gpt-oss-120b by default) and follows a tool-based workflow with four tools:

Search products
Add products to the cart
Check spending policy
Request human approval

The agent has no payment creation or capture tool, so it cannot charge the user. If the model is unavailable, a scripted no-AI fallback runs the same flow with the same policy and ledger.

The spending policy is implemented separately from the LLM, so financial decisions are deterministic and don't depend on AI-generated text.

For checkout, I integrated PayPal Orders v2 on the server and the PayPal JavaScript SDK v6 in the browser. Payment amounts are always calculated server-side from the stored cart. The policy is re-checked at approval and again at capture, so changing the cart or the rules can't slip past the restrictions.

After capture, the server asks the official PayPal MCP server for the order using get_order. If that lookup fails, it falls back to a PayPal REST API lookup. The verification result is recorded in the ledger.

I also implemented a PayPal webhook handler with signature verification and event deduplication. Webhook registration and live delivery were not tested during the demo.

The demo uses a seeded mock catalog of 40 products, including restricted categories such as gift cards, alcohol and weapons, so the blocked-category rules can be shown. An optional Channel3 integration is in the code but was not used in the demo.

The app is deployed on Render, and the source code is public on GitHub. The hosted demo uses a single shared sandbox ledger and monthly budget with no user accounts, and its database resets on each deploy.

Challenges I ran into

My biggest challenge was keeping a strict separation between AI reasoning and financial operations. The LLM had to be able to suggest purchases and request approval without ever being able to create or capture a payment.

Integrating PayPal's JavaScript SDK v6 meant adapting to its different order-creation contract, where the order promise is passed to session.start().

The PayPal MCP get_order tool expected a different argument name than I first used, so I made MCP errors surface and added a REST fallback.

I also had to design the approval and capture workflow so that spending policies are re-evaluated at each critical stage and the same order cannot be processed twice.

Finally, I thought about how restricted categories would be identified with a live product catalog, since external categories may not match my own policy categories.

Accomplishments that I'm proud of
An agent that is structurally unable to spend money: it has no payment or capture tool, and amounts come only from the stored cart.
A deterministic policy engine that blocks bad carts, explains exactly which rule was hit with the numbers, and lets the agent propose a compliant alternative.
Policy re-checks at approval and at capture, so a changed cart or changed rules can't slip a purchase through.
An end-to-end PayPal sandbox payment, verified afterwards and recorded in a ledger you can filter and inspect.
A scripted fallback, so the same guarded flow still works if the AI model is unavailable.
What I learned

Building a trustworthy AI agent takes more than choosing a capable language model.

I learned how to connect an LLM to structured tools, enforce policy deterministically, build server-side payment workflows, work with the PayPal Sandbox, keep an auditable ledger, and verify payments after capture.

Most importantly, I learned that AI autonomy does not have to mean unrestricted authority. An agent can be useful and proactive while staying inside boundaries enforced by independent software and human approval.

What's next for Errand Agent: AI shopping agent with PayPal guardrails

I plan to add per-merchant and per-category budgets, live product and delivery information, multi-user authentication, spending anomaly alerts, and a human-controlled policy exception workflow.

My long-term goal is to make AI-powered errands convenient without making people give up control of their money.
